newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: More protests to hit US soy ships in Europe.
newsitem.headline: More protests to hit US soy ships in Europe.

text.p: Ships carrying a new strain of genetically-altered American soybeans to Europe's food industry will continue to hit a wall of protest when they dock, environmental activists said on Wednesday.

Amsterdam-based Greenpeace International has vowed to keep up a campaign of direct action against the imports following Tuesday's arrival of the freighter Ideal Progress in Hamburg -- the first ship believed to be carrying the new beans.
"We were involved in the direct action in Hamburg and we will definitely be following that up," Greenpeace International spokesman Jon Walter told Reuters.
Several more vessels are expected to arrive in the ports of Antwerp, Ghent and Rotterdam over the coming weeks.

The Ideal Progress, which left New Orleans three weeks ago, was met by the Greenpeace barge Beluga, which tried to prevent it from docking. Activists used slide projectors to emblazon its hull with slogans such as "We are not your guinea pigs".
After police intervention, the ship and its cargo of 44,600 tonnes of U.S. soybeans docked successfully.

The group said the vessel was carrying the new type of bean, which has been developed by U.S. chemicals group Monsanto to be resistant to its own new "super weedkiller" Roundup. Environmental groups describe the Roundup technology as a risky experiment with nature.
But the new Monsanto strain has been given a clean bill of health by the authorities in the United States and European Union, who say it poses no danger to the human food chain.
Moreover, they stress its environmental benefits, saying fewer types of pesticides need to be used during cultivation.
Every week in Europe thousands of tonnes of soybeans are processed into meal and oil, which is used in a wide variety of everyday foods such as margarine, chocolate and mayonnaise.
The Greenpeace campaign has also focused on raising consumer awareness ouside Germany, where the fears are most acute.
"The big European food processors are starting to feel the consumer pressure. This is going to build," Walter said.
However national bodies like the Dutch Food and Drink Industry Association have endorsed the product, saying their members would use genetically-altered soya.
"This month, soybeans will be imported into the Netherlands which have been produced with the help of modern bio-technology.
"The Dutch food sector only processes and sells products that are safe for the consumer and which have government approval," it said in a statement this week.
But campaigners want processors at the very least to separate the beans from conventionally-grown ones and so give consumers a choice of buying products that have not been genetically manipulated.
Separation has so far proved unworkable as the two types are mixed together in huge U.S. grain silos before shipment.
German Social Democrat MP Klaus Lennartz on Wednesday called for a consumer boycott of products containing the new beans, unless clear labelling was provided.
"Consumers should refuse to buy products containing soya as long as the food industry refuses to indicate voluntarily traces of genetic modification," he said from his Bonn office.
U.S. consumer activist Jeremy Rifkin, who is seeking a world boycott of genetically-altered grain, arrived in Germany this week to declare that "this global boycott will not go away."
He said grain handlers in the U.S. Midwest had already begun to negotiate contracts for supplying unmodified beans to those who did not want the Monsanto soy.
Some leading European firms, including the German unit of Anglo-Dutch Unilever, have bowed to consumer pressure and announced they will not use the new variety even though they consider it safe.
